data.title: The Child's Bath

thumbnail.alt_text: Painting of mother in blue, purple, and green-stripped dress washing child's feet.

data.description:
In The Child’s Bath, Cassatt centered two figures in a moment of physical closeness: a woman steadies a young charge on her lap as she holds the child’s foot in the washbasin below. The steep angle from above creates a shallow picture plane, pulling viewers into the space. The carpeted floor seems to sit upright on the surface of the canvas. Adding to this sense of flatness, pattern is everywhere within the frame. These formal elements reflect Cassatt’s intense engagement with Japanese aesthetics in the 1890s.

An extraordinary composition featuring the artist’s signature subject, The Child’s Bath was widely exhibited beginning in 1893. The Art Institute of Chicago purchased the painting in 1910—making it the first work by Cassatt to enter the museum’s collection.
data.short_description: Known for her sensitive yet unsentimental scenes of women and children, Mary Cassatt was the only American invited to exhibit with the original French Impressionist group. In The Child’s Bath, one of her masterworks, she used cropped forms, bold patterns and outlines, and a flattened perspective, all of which she derived from her study of Japanese woodblock prints.
data.inscriptions: Signed recto, bottom-left, on floor, in blue paint:  "Mary Cassatt".

data.provenance_text: The artist; sold to Galeries Durand-Ruel, Paris, Nov. 24, 1893 [Galeries Durand-Ruel 1893, cat. 1; this and the following according to letter from Charles Durand-Ruel, Jan. 30, 1979; copy in curatorial object file]; sold to Durand-Ruel Galleries (Durand-Ruel & Son Galleries), New York, Dec. 27, 1893; sold to (Arthur) Harris Whittemore, Jr. (1864–1927), Naugatuck, CT, Jan. 17, 1894 [personal communication from Flavie Durand-Ruel and Caroline Durand-Ruel Godfroy, Mar. 23, 2026; copy in curatorial object file]; sold to Durand-Ruel, New York, Feb. 4, 1899; sold to the Art Institute of Chicago, 1910.
